name: Cybersecurity
tagline: High demand, high pay — and much harder to enter than the ads claim.
description: Security operations is a real, well-paid career that people reach without a degree. It is also the single most oversold path in tech: bootcamp marketing implies you can go from zero to $90K in six months, and that essentially never happens. Security is a second job, not a first one. The people who get SOC analyst roles almost always come from help desk, sysadmin, or networking first.
avgTimeline: 18–30 months realistically, usually via IT support or networking first

salaryRange.note: Entry SOC Analyst (Tier 1) range. BLS reports a $124,910 median for information security analysts (May 2024) — that is a mid-to-senior number and is the figure ads quote at beginners. Tier 1 SOC work, often on rotating shifts, is where you actually start.

remoteFriendly.note: SOC work is monitoring and analysis, so it remotes well and many SOCs are fully remote — but expect shift work, including nights and weekends, because attacks do not observe business hours.

realityCheck: Entry-level cybersecurity is largely a myth as a first job. Most 'entry-level' SOC postings ask for 1–2 years of IT experience, and they mean it. The path below is honest about that: get help desk or networking experience while you build security skills, then move.
whyItFits: If you're the person who notices when something is off — the count doesn't match, the process was skipped, the story doesn't add up — that instinct is the core of the job. The technical knowledge is learnable; the attention isn't.

motivation.quote: There is no shortage of people who want cybersecurity jobs. There is a shortage of people who can actually do the work. Be the second kind and the market opens up.
motivation.story: The realistic version of this story takes about two years: help desk for a year while running TryHackMe rooms at night, an internal move to a security-adjacent role (patching, vulnerability remediation, access reviews), then a Tier 1 SOC job. People who skip straight to applying for SOC roles with only a Security+ typically send 200 applications and get nothing — the same person after 12 months of help desk gets interviews.
motivation.source: Composite of the pattern consistently reported in r/cybersecurity 'how I got in' threads

interviewPrep.question: You get an alert for a successful login from a new country. Walk me through your triage.
interviewPrep.why: The core SOC interview question. Structure: verify the alert is real, check the user's normal pattern, check for impossible travel, look for what happened after login, check MFA logs, decide escalate vs. close as benign, document everything.

interviewPrep.question: Explain the CIA triad and give a real example of each being violated.
interviewPrep.why: Basic but always asked. Confidentiality: data breach. Integrity: tampered records. Availability: ransomware or DDoS.

interviewPrep.question: How does a phishing attack actually lead to a breach?
interviewPrep.why: Walk the chain: credential capture or malicious attachment → initial access → persistence → privilege escalation → lateral movement → objective. Mentioning the MITRE ATT&CK framework by name here helps.

interviewPrep.question: What is a SIEM and what do you use it for?
interviewPrep.why: Centralized log aggregation, correlation, and alerting. Name one you've touched — Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, Elastic — even from a free lab.

interviewPrep.question: What's the difference between an IDS and an IPS? Where does a firewall fit?
interviewPrep.why: IDS detects and alerts, IPS blocks inline, firewall enforces policy at the boundary. This question is really checking whether you have networking fundamentals under the security vocabulary.

interviewPrep.question: How would you determine whether a suspicious file is malicious?
interviewPrep.why: Hash lookup against VirusTotal, static analysis (strings, headers), detonation in an isolated sandbox, check for known IOCs. Say explicitly that you would not run it on a production machine.

interviewPrep.question: You closed an alert as benign and it turned out to be a real incident. What do you do?
interviewPrep.why: They're testing whether you hide mistakes. The right answer is fast escalation, full disclosure of your reasoning, and a detection-improvement suggestion afterward.

steps.title: Build the IT and networking foundation first
steps.description: Security is applied IT. You cannot analyze suspicious network traffic without knowing what normal traffic looks like, and you cannot spot a malicious process without knowing which processes belong. Do A+ and Network+ (or work a support job for a year) before spending money on security certs. This is the step people skip and then wonder why nobody calls back.
steps.estimatedTime: 6–12 months (overlaps with the IT Support / Networking paths)
steps.costNote: Costs are counted on the IT Support and Networking paths, not double-counted here.
steps.outcome: Working IT knowledge, ideally with a support job on the resume.

resources.name: IT Support / Help Desk path (this site)
resources.notes: Internal — the standard prerequisite.

resources.name: Networking / SysAdmin path (this site)
resources.notes: Internal — Network+ level knowledge is assumed by every security role.

steps.title: Work through free security fundamentals training
steps.description: Start with structured free material before paying for anything. TryHackMe's beginner paths teach real tooling in a browser — no local install, which means much of this works on a library computer. Learn the vocabulary: threat, vulnerability, risk, IOC, CVE, least privilege, defense in depth.
steps.costNote: Free tier is genuinely usable. TryHackMe's paid tier is about $14/month if you want the full paths — reasonable, but exhaust the free rooms first.
steps.outcome: Comfort with core security concepts and hands-on time in browser-based labs.
steps.resumeBullet: Completed hands-on security fundamentals labs covering network analysis, log review, and threat identification (TryHackMe).

resources.name: TryHackMe — free beginner rooms and Pre-Security path
resources.notes: Substantial free content; subscription ~$14/month unlocks the rest. Runs entirely in a browser, which makes it unusually accessible.

resources.name: Professor Messer — free Security+ video course
resources.notes: Free. Doubles as your Security+ prep later. Confirm the current exam code before starting.

resources.name: MITRE ATT&CK framework
resources.notes: Free. Learn to navigate it — interviewers ask about it and analysts reference it daily.

resources.name: Cisco Networking Academy — free Introduction to Cybersecurity
resources.notes: Free with a certificate of completion.

steps.title: Pass CompTIA Security+
steps.description: Security+ is the baseline credential for this field. It matters for two concrete reasons beyond knowledge: it satisfies the US DoD 8140/8570 IAT Level II requirement, which unlocks a large government-contractor job market, and it clears HR keyword filters. It will not, by itself, get you a SOC job.
steps.costNote: PAID: roughly $439 as of CompTIA's June 2026 pricing. Check for partner vouchers and student discounts. If you are a US veteran, VA benefits and programs like VET TEC frequently cover this entirely.
steps.resumeBullet: CompTIA Security+ certified — threat analysis, risk management, cryptography fundamentals, identity and access management, and incident response.

resources.name: CompTIA Security+ official page
resources.notes: PAID. Confirm the live exam code and price before buying — CompTIA raised prices June 1, 2026.

resources.name: Jason Dion Security+ practice exams (Udemy)
resources.notes: PAID, typically $15–20 on sale. Score 85%+ consistently before booking the real exam.

resources.name: r/CompTIA Security+ pass threads
resources.notes: Free. People post their exact study stacks and timelines.

steps.title: Practice blue-team work in realistic labs
steps.description: SOC work is defense, not hacking. Spend your lab time on the defensive side: reading logs, investigating alerts, triaging phishing emails, writing up incidents. LetsDefend and Blue Team Labs Online simulate an actual SOC queue, which is far more relevant to your first job than capture-the-flag hacking challenges.
steps.costNote: Free tiers on LetsDefend, Blue Team Labs Online, and CyberDefenders cover a lot. Paid tiers run $20–40/month — worth one or two months when you're actively interviewing, not before.
steps.outcome: Documented investigations you can walk an interviewer through.
steps.resumeBullet: Completed 25+ simulated SOC investigations (LetsDefend, Blue Team Labs Online): alert triage, log correlation, phishing analysis, and written incident reports.

resources.name: LetsDefend — browser-based SOC analyst simulation
resources.notes: Free tier with real alert-queue simulation; paid plans around $25–30/month. Browser-based.

resources.name: Blue Team Labs Online
resources.notes: Free investigations available; paid tier for the full catalogue.

resources.name: CyberDefenders
resources.notes: Free blue-team challenges built on real packet captures and disk images.

resources.name: Hack The Box (offensive side, optional)
resources.notes: Free tier available; ~$14/month for VIP. Fun and useful for understanding attacker behavior, but less directly relevant to a first defensive job than the blue-team platforms above.

steps.title: Build a home SOC: logs, SIEM, and detection
steps.description: Stand up a small detection lab: a Windows VM sending logs, a free SIEM collecting them, and a few attack simulations you run against yourself. Wazuh or Security Onion are free and this is the project that most convincingly separates you from people who only have certificates.
steps.costNote: Free. Wazuh, Security Onion, Elastic's free tier, and Microsoft Sentinel's free trial credit all cost nothing. Needs a machine with 16GB RAM ideally.
steps.outcome: A working SIEM ingesting real logs, with detections you wrote and tested.
steps.resumeBullet: Built a home SOC lab: deployed Wazuh/Security Onion SIEM, forwarded Windows and Linux telemetry, simulated attacks with Atomic Red Team, and authored custom detection rules.

resources.name: Wazuh (free open-source SIEM/XDR)
resources.notes: Free and open source. The most common free home-SIEM choice.

resources.name: Security Onion
resources.notes: Free. A full network-security-monitoring distribution — heavier, very realistic.

resources.name: Atomic Red Team (safe attack simulation)
resources.notes: Free, open source. Run mapped ATT&CK techniques against your own lab to test whether your detections fire.

resources.name: Microsoft Sentinel free trial + SC-900 learning path
resources.notes: Free training. Sentinel is very widely used, so hands-on time is directly employable.

steps.title: Write up your investigations publicly
steps.description: Security hiring rewards visible thinking more than most fields. Publish 5–10 short writeups — an investigation you completed, a detection you wrote, a lab you built — on a free blog or GitHub. Hiring managers read these. It is also the cheapest way to compensate for not having a degree or a security job yet.
steps.costNote: Free. GitHub Pages, Medium, and dev.to all cost nothing.
steps.outcome: A public body of work with your name on it.
steps.resumeBullet: Published technical writeups on detection engineering and incident investigation, documenting methodology and findings.

resources.name: GitHub Pages (free static hosting)
resources.notes: Free. Also gives you a GitHub profile, which recruiters check.

resources.name: dev.to
resources.notes: Free publishing with a built-in technical audience.

steps.title: Move sideways into security from an IT role
steps.description: The highest-probability route into a security job is from inside a company that already employs you. Volunteer for the security-adjacent work nobody wants: patch compliance, access reviews, phishing report triage, vulnerability remediation tickets. Twelve months of that plus Security+ makes you a credible internal candidate — and internal candidates skip most of the competition.
steps.costNote: Free — this happens on company time.
steps.outcome: Security responsibilities on your current job description.
steps.resumeBullet: Owned security-adjacent operational work including patch compliance reporting, user access reviews, and phishing report triage.

resources.name: r/cybersecurity — 'breaking in' megathreads
resources.notes: Free. Read the mentorship monday threads for unvarnished expectations.

resources.name: Local BSides / OWASP chapter meetups
resources.notes: Free or very cheap. In-person security meetups are one of the few places a no-degree candidate reliably meets hiring managers.

steps.title: Apply to SOC Tier 1 and security analyst roles
steps.description: Target managed security service providers (MSSPs) — they run large SOCs, hire Tier 1 continuously, and accept less experience than in-house teams. Accept that shift work is likely. Also consider GRC and compliance analyst roles: less technical, less competitive, and a legitimate way into the field for someone with strong process and documentation habits.

resources.name: Indeed — SOC analyst listings
resources.notes: Free. Also search 'security operations', 'MSSP analyst', 'GRC analyst', and 'security specialist'.

resources.name: ClearanceJobs (government contracting)
resources.notes: Free to browse. Security+ plus clearance sponsorship is one of the most reliable no-degree routes into security in the US.

resources.name: NICE Cybersecurity Workforce Framework (role definitions)
resources.notes: Free US government framework describing what each security role actually does — useful for figuring out which titles to target.
